newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian orphans guard gates to their home.
newsitem.headline: Albanian orphans guard gates to their home.

text.p: Orphans guard the gate to their home as gunfire crackles along the waterfront in the southern Albanian port city of Sarande.

Aphrodite, 11, marches back and forth with a bit of scrap lumber carved in the shape of a Kalashnikov slung over his shoulder. Suleyman, 13, carries a faded red and black Albanian flag on a splintered staff.
"We are the guards. Our job is to stand here by this gate to make sure the gunmen don't enter," Suleyman confided.
The orphans' vigil is make-believe, but at night adults take over in deadly earnest.
"I am here at night patrolling with my Kalashnikov because these are my children and I am their father," explained Petro Qurko, the director of Sarande's orphanage.

"Gangs have tried to steal our food and occupy our building. Refugees have tried to move in. I told them that I would shoot to kill. If they came to my house I would not shoot, but the orphanage is different. These children have nothing else."
Staff at the orphanage have not been paid for two months. Bread is being donated by a local bakery. Neighbours pitch in to help guard the institution at night.
"We have food for another 20 days but at some point we are going to need money from the government," the director said.

"There is a limit to how long we can expect to survive on the generosity of private citizens. The Mayor of Athens came a few days ago and promised us whatever supplies we needed but he said the situation would have to calm down first."
Like many towns in Albania, especially in the south, Sarande is gripped by lawlessness.
The recent collapse of a number of pyramid schemes bankrupted many Albanian families, sparking anti-government protests and widespread civil unrest including looting.
There is virtually no government presence in the south and public institutions like the Sarande orphanage are proving most vulnerable to the chaos swirling around them.
"I haven't been outside the orphanage for two months. It's like being in prison," complained 14-year old Elefteria Kito.
"I miss seeing my friends at school and in the town. The shooting at night keeps me awake. I'm feeling very isolated. No bullets have hit our building but we have had some shrapnel land in the yard."
Orphanage staff say the home's 90 children are becoming restless and that behaviour problems are getting worse.
Basic meals remain adequate but there is no money to buy fruit or vegetables to balance the children's diet.
Detergents needed to clean bathrooms and wash clothes properly remain in short supply.

On a day when small arms and machine-gun fire rips the air above Sarande some orphans remain oblivious as they sit in a second floor TV room watching a violent Japanese Kung-Fu movie dubbed into English and sub-titled in Albanian.
"There is so much craziness in the world it must affect our children," Petro Qurku, the director, worried.
"My own 14-year old son came home one day with a Kalashnikov he had stolen when the town's army depot was looted."
"I yelled at him and told him we were a normal family with no need of guns. But now I have to use the stolem Kalashnikov to patrol the orphanage at night. What can I say to my son?"
